title: Routing and app structure
intro: A real application usually has more than one screen, even when it is built as a single-page application. In this lesson, you will learn how client-side routing connects URLs to React components, how React Router handles navigation, and how to organise a small React application as it grows.
body:
## Why routing is needed A simple React application might display one component and never change the URL. But a real application usually has several screens: - A home page. - A task list. - A task details page. - A profile page. - A settings page. - A login page. You could manually keep track of which screen should be visible with React state. That can work for a tiny application, but it quickly becomes difficult to manage. Users also expect the browser URL to represent where they are. For example: ~~~text / /tasks /tasks/42 /about ~~~ If someone copies `/tasks/42` and sends it to another person, the application should be able to open that specific task page. **Client-side routing** connects URLs to parts of a React application without requiring the browser to perform a full page navigation for every route. This is particularly useful for a **single-page application**, or SPA. An SPA normally loads the main application once and then changes the displayed content as the user navigates. --- ## React Router React itself does not provide a full routing system. A commonly used library is **React Router**. ~~~diagram {"type": "flow", "title": "The URL picks the screen", "nodes": [{"id": "url", "label": "/tasks/42", "kind": "client"}, {"id": "r", "label": "", "kind": "code", "highlight": true}, {"id": "lay", "label": "", "sub": "header + "}, {"id": "list", "label": "/tasks → TasksPage"}, {"id": "det", "label": "/tasks/:id → TaskDetail", "sub": "useParams() → { id: '42' }", "highlight": true}, {"id": "nf", "label": "* → NotFound"}], "edges": [{"from": "url", "to": "r"}, {"from": "r", "to": "lay"}, {"from": "lay", "to": "list", "dashed": true}, {"from": "lay", "to": "det", "label": "match"}, {"from": "lay", "to": "nf", "dashed": true}]} ~~~ In a real project, you install it as a dependency and define routes that connect URLs to components. One modern approach uses `createBrowserRouter`: ~~~jsx import { createBrowserRouter, RouterProvider } from "react-router"; const router = createBrowserRouter([ { path: "/", element: }, { path: "/tasks", element: } ]); function App() { return ; } ~~~ Another familiar API uses `BrowserRouter`, `Routes`, and `Route`: ~~~jsx import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from "react-router"; function App() { return ( } /> } /> ); } ~~~ The exact API you choose depends on the React Router version and the architecture of your application. The underlying idea is the same: **a URL is matched to a React component tree**. --- ## Link instead of normal navigation Once you have routes, you usually do not want normal HTML links to reload the entire application. React Router provides `Link`: ~~~jsx import { Link } from "react-router"; function Navigation() { return (
Home Tasks About
); } ~~~ When the user clicks a `Link`, React Router changes the browser URL and displays the matching route without performing a normal full-page navigation. This is one of the important differences between: ~~~html Tasks ~~~ and: ~~~jsx Tasks ~~~ A normal anchor is a browser navigation. `Link` lets the router handle the navigation inside the SPA. --- ## NavLink and active navigation Navigation often needs to show which page is currently active. React Router provides `NavLink` for this purpose: ~~~jsx import { NavLink } from "react-router"; function Navigation() { return (
Home Tasks About
); } ~~~ `NavLink` knows whether its route is active and can provide an active state to your styling logic. For example: ~~~jsx isActive ? "active" : ""} > Tasks ~~~ You can also use the active state to add an accessibility attribute: ~~~jsx isActive ? "page" : undefined} > Tasks ~~~ This makes it clear which navigation item represents the current page. --- ## URL parameters A route can contain a dynamic part. Imagine a task details page: ~~~jsx } /> ~~~ The `:id` part is a **route parameter**. It can match values such as: ~~~text /tasks/1 /tasks/42 /tasks/abc ~~~ The component can read the parameter using `useParams`: ~~~jsx import { useParams } from "react-router"; function TaskDetails() { const { id } = useParams(); return

Task {id}

; } ~~~ If the browser is currently at `/tasks/42`, `id` will contain `42`. In a real application, you could then use that ID to request the corresponding task from your API. For example: ~~~jsx function TaskDetails() { const { id } = useParams(); // Load task with this id... return

Task {id}

; } ~~~ The route parameter connects the URL to the data the page needs. --- ## Programmatic navigation Sometimes navigation should happen because of application logic rather than a user clicking a link. For example, after successfully logging in, you might want to navigate to the dashboard. React Router provides `useNavigate`: ~~~jsx import { useNavigate } from "react-router"; function Login() { const navigate = useNavigate(); function handleLogin() { // Login logic... navigate("/dashboard"); } return ; } ~~~ You can also navigate backwards: ~~~jsx navigate(-1); ~~~ This is useful for actions such as a Cancel button or returning to the previous screen. Use normal links for normal navigation when possible. `useNavigate` is most useful when navigation is a consequence of some application event or logic. --- ## A 404 route Users will eventually visit a URL that does not exist. A router can provide a catch-all route for this: ~~~jsx } /> } /> } /> ~~~ The `*` route catches paths that did not match another route. The component might be simple: ~~~jsx function NotFound() { return (

Page not found

Back home
); } ~~~ A proper 404 page is much better than leaving users with a blank screen when they enter an invalid URL. --- ## Nested layouts Larger applications often have a common layout around several pages. For example, an application might have the same header and navigation on every page: ~~~text App layout ├── Header ├── Navigation └── Page content ├── Home ├── Tasks └── About ~~~ React Router supports this through nested routes and `Outlet`. A layout can contain: ~~~jsx import { Outlet } from "react-router"; function AppLayout() { return ( <>
My application
{/* navigation */}
); } ~~~ The `Outlet` is the place where the currently matched child route is rendered. A route configuration could look like: ~~~jsx const router = createBrowserRouter([ { path: "/", element: , children: [ { index: true, element: }, { path: "tasks", element: }, { path: "about", element: } ] } ]); ~~~ This lets you share the layout without duplicating the header and navigation in every page. --- ## Routing and the server There is an important deployment detail with client-side routing. ~~~callout warn Refreshing gives a 404? React Router runs in the browser, but a refresh asks the **server** for `/tasks/42`. Configure the host to send `index.html` for unknown paths (a SPA fallback), or every deep link breaks. ~~~ Imagine your React application is deployed at: ~~~text https://example.com ~~~ The user can navigate inside the application to: ~~~text https://example.com/tasks/42 ~~~ React Router understands that URL. But what happens if the user refreshes the browser while already on `/tasks/42`? The browser asks the server for `/tasks/42`. If the server only knows how to serve `/`, it might respond with a 404. For an SPA, the server generally needs to serve the application's `index.html` for client-side routes that should be handled by React. Then React starts in the browser and React Router handles the `/tasks/42` route. This becomes especially important when you deploy a React frontend alongside a **Spring Boot** backend later in the course. Your deployment needs to distinguish between API requests such as `/api/tasks` and frontend routes such as `/tasks/42`. The exact server configuration depends on how you deploy the application, but the core issue is always the same: **the browser needs to receive the React application for a client-side route before React Router can handle that route**. --- ## A useful project structure As your React application grows, keeping everything in one `App.jsx` becomes difficult. A small application could use a structure like: ~~~text src/ api/ tasks.js components/ Header.jsx TaskCard.jsx TaskList.jsx hooks/ useTasks.js pages/ Home.jsx Tasks.jsx TaskDetails.jsx About.jsx App.jsx main.jsx ~~~ The folders have different responsibilities. `pages/` contains components that represent application screens or route-level views. `components/` contains reusable UI pieces that can be used by multiple pages. `api/` contains code responsible for communicating with backend APIs. `hooks/` contains reusable React hooks, such as a hook that loads and manages task data. This is not a mandatory React structure. You can organise projects differently. The important principle is to give files clear responsibilities and avoid putting unrelated concerns into one giant component. --- ## Lazy-loading pages Large applications do not necessarily need to download every page's JavaScript when the application first loads. React supports lazy-loading components with `lazy` and `Suspense`, allowing route-level code to be loaded when it is needed. React Router can be combined with this approach so that, for example, an administration page is downloaded only when the user navigates to it, reducing the initial JavaScript payload. A simplified example looks like: ~~~jsx import { lazy, Suspense } from "react"; const About = lazy(() => import("./pages/About")); function App() { return ( Loading...

}> ); } ~~~ You do not need lazy-loading for every small application. It becomes more useful as the application and its JavaScript bundle grow. --- ## Routing without a router It is useful to understand what a router is doing underneath all the abstractions. At its simplest, you could store the current page in React state: ~~~jsx const [page, setPage] = React.useState("home"); ~~~ Then render different content based on that state: ~~~jsx {page === "home" && } {page === "tasks" && } {page === "about" && } ~~~ This is not a complete routing solution because it does not automatically integrate with browser URLs, history, dynamic parameters, nested layouts, or deep links. But it demonstrates the basic idea: **some piece of routing state determines which UI should be displayed**. The exercise in this lesson uses exactly this simplified approach because the course sandbox does not provide React Router. In a real project, a routing library gives you the features needed to turn this basic idea into a proper URL-based navigation system. --- ## Common mistakes ### Using state instead of a router for a real application A state-based page switcher can be useful for learning or very small interfaces, but a multi-page application usually benefits from a real routing solution with URLs, browser history, parameters, and nested routes. ### Using normal anchors for every internal navigation A normal `` causes browser navigation. Use React Router's `Link` or `NavLink` for internal SPA navigation when you are using React Router. ### Forgetting dynamic parameters A route such as `/tasks/:id` allows one component to handle many task URLs. Use `useParams` to read the actual value. ### Forgetting the server configuration A route can work perfectly when navigating inside the application but fail after refreshing a deep URL. The server needs to serve the React application's entry HTML for client-side routes. ### Putting every component into one folder As the application grows, separate route-level pages, reusable components, API code, and custom hooks so each part has a clear responsibility. ### Using programmatic navigation everywhere If the user is simply clicking a navigation link, use `Link` or `NavLink`. Use `useNavigate` when navigation is triggered by application logic such as completing a login or saving a form. --- ## The bigger picture Routing connects the browser's URL with the component tree shown to the user. React Router adds the infrastructure for navigation links, active navigation, dynamic parameters, programmatic navigation, 404 pages, and shared layouts. A good React application usually separates route-level pages from reusable components and keeps API and reusable hook logic in their own areas. As the application grows, lazy-loading can also reduce the amount of JavaScript that needs to be downloaded initially. The important thing to remember is that routing is more than switching between components. It connects **URLs, browser history, application state, and the component tree** into one navigation system.
takeaways: Client-side routing lets a single-page React application display different screens while keeping navigation connected to browser URLs.
React Router provides tools such as Routes, Route, Link, NavLink, useParams, useNavigate, and Outlet for common routing problems.
Dynamic routes such as /tasks/:id let one component handle many URLs and useParams provides the actual route parameter.
When deploying an SPA, the server must serve the application's index.html for client-side routes so React Router can handle deep links.
Separating pages, reusable components, API code, and hooks makes a React application easier to understand and maintain as it grows.

quiz.question: Why does a single-page React application need client-side routing?
options: To make CSS load faster
To connect different URLs to different parts of the React application without a full page navigation
To replace JavaScript with HTML
To store data in a database
quiz.explanation: Client-side routing lets an SPA respond to URLs and display the appropriate React UI without performing a traditional full-page navigation for every route.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of NavLink compared with Link?
options: NavLink can detect whether its route is currently active
NavLink can only be used for external websites
NavLink replaces all React components
NavLink automatically fetches backend data
quiz.explanation: NavLink provides information about whether its destination is active, which is useful for active navigation styles and attributes such as aria-current.

quiz.question: What value does useParams provide for the route /tasks/:id?
options: The complete React component tree
The current browser history object only
The value matched by the id route parameter
The list of all registered routes
quiz.explanation: useParams gives the values captured by dynamic route segments. For /tasks/42, the id parameter would contain 42.

quiz.question: What does Outlet do in a nested React Router layout?
options: It redirects the browser to another domain
It is the place where the matched child route is rendered
It stores route parameters in localStorage
It creates a new browser tab
quiz.explanation: Outlet marks the location inside a parent layout where the currently matched child route should be rendered.

quiz.question: Why can a deployed React app return a 404 when refreshing /tasks/42 even though navigation to that route worked inside the app?
options: React cannot render URLs containing numbers
The browser disables React after a refresh
The server may not be configured to serve index.html for the client-side route
useParams only works before a refresh
quiz.explanation: A browser refresh sends /tasks/42 directly to the server. If the server does not serve the React entry HTML for that route, it can return a 404 before React Router gets a chance to handle the URL.

exercise.title: Build a tiny state-based router
exercise.task: Build an `App` component that acts as a tiny router using React state because the sandbox does not provide a routing library. Render a `nav` containing three buttons with the exact texts `Home`, `Tasks`, and `About`, and keep the current page in state with `home` as the initial value. The active navigation button must have `aria-current="page"`, while inactive buttons must not have an `aria-current` attribute. Inside a `main` element, render `home` as an `h1` with exactly `Welcome`, `tasks` as an `h1` with exactly `Tasks` followed by a `ul` containing `Buy milk` and `Write tests`, and `about` as an `h1` with exactly `About`. Clicking either task item must show a `p` with `data-testid="detail"` containing exactly `Task: <title>`; switching to another page should remove that detail. The tests click the navigation and task buttons and then check the headings, active state, and detail text.
exercise.hint: Keep the current page in one state variable and use conditional rendering inside main. Use a second state value for the selected task title, and clear it whenever navigation changes. For the active button, set aria-current to page only when its page matches the current state; otherwise pass undefined so the attribute is absent.

tests.name: starts on Home with the correct active navigation
clicking Tasks shows the task page and changes active navigation
clicking a task shows its detail
clicking another task updates the detail
clicking About shows About and removes task detail
clicking Home returns to Welcome
